steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Blue notes (flattened 3rd, 5th and 7th of the major scale) create the characteristic blues sound — they fall between the notes of the Western scale.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: 12-bar blues follows a I-IV-V chord progression over three four-bar phrases: the AAB lyric structure mirrors this harmonic pattern.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Call and response between vocalist and guitar/harp creates dialogue — a fundamental feature inherited from African musical traditions.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Shuffle rhythm (long-short subdivision of the beat) gives blues its distinctive swing feel — it is notated in 12/8 or with triplets in 4/4.

steps.body: A detailed description using precise musical vocabulary (e.g. specific terms from the AQA elements list), referencing a named piece with accurate observations about how the elements are used and their | A comparison of two pieces identifying similarities and differences in how blues music 1920-1950 are used, explaining the different effects created in each musical context, using comparative language. | A practical application showing understanding of how blues music 1920-1950 can be manipulated in composition or performance, with specific examples of choices made and their intended effect.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always use PRECISE musical vocabulary — not vague descriptions like it sounds nice Reference SPECIFIC musical elements when analysing any piece For listening questions: identify elements FIRST, then explain their effect For study pieces: know the context, structure and key features in detail For performing: focus on accuracy, expression and interpretation For composing: show development of ideas, not just repetition
